questions.question: A Product Owner is deciding the order of the product backlog. On what basis should items be ordered?
questions.explanation: In Scrum the Product Owner is accountable for ordering the backlog. Ordering reflects overall business priority - the Product Owner typically weighs value together with risk, urgency, dependencies, and effort rather than any single factor. These are considerations the Product Owner balances, not a fixed universal formula; ordering by value alone, by title, or by individual preference misses them.  Takeaway: The Product Owner orders the backlog by overall business priority - weighing value with risk, urgency, and dependencies, not value alone.
choices: The personal preference of the newest developer
Business priority, weighing value along with risk, urgency, and dependencies
Alphabetical order of the item titles
Only the raw dollar value, ignoring all other factors

questions.question: A buyer is selecting a contract type for a well-defined scope of work. Which statements about how contract types allocate cost risk are correct?
questions.explanation: In an FFP contract the price is set, so the seller absorbs cost overruns for the agreed scope. Under CPFF the buyer reimburses allowable costs plus a fixed fee, keeping cost risk with the buyer. T&M cost rises with hours worked, and cost-plus prices are less predictable for the buyer, so the other options reverse the actual risk allocation.  Takeaway: Fixed-price contracts push cost risk to the seller, while cost-plus and T&M contracts leave more cost risk with the buyer.
choices: Under a firm-fixed-price (FFP) contract, the seller bears the risk of cost overruns for the agreed scope.
Under a time-and-materials (T&M) contract, the buyer's total cost is fixed regardless of the hours worked.
Under a cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF) contract, the buyer reimburses allowable costs plus a set fee and carries more cost risk.
A firm-fixed-price contract places the risk of cost overruns on the buyer rather than the seller.
A cost-plus contract gives the buyer a lower and more predictable final price than a fixed-price contract.

questions.question: A product team debates what its first release should contain. Which description best matches a minimum viable product (MVP)?
questions.explanation: An MVP is the smallest usable version that lets the team test assumptions with real users and gain validated learning. It is not defined as the full set of Must-have items, and it is a real releasable slice rather than a discarded prototype.  Takeaway: MVP is the smallest release that enables validated learning, not all the Must-haves.
choices: Every requirement labeled Must-have under MoSCoW, all released together
A throwaway prototype that is deliberately never placed in front of real users
The smallest version that real users can use so the team can gain validated learning
A fully polished release with all planned features so that rework is avoided later

questions.question: A predictive project manager argues that business analysis only matters on agile projects. Which statement best corrects this view?
questions.explanation: Business analysis is a set of activities carried out across the whole life cycle in both predictive and adaptive approaches, so it is not limited to agile. It is not confined to a single planning event, and it complements rather than replaces the project manager.  Takeaway: Business analysis happens across the whole life cycle in both predictive and adaptive approaches.
choices: Business analysis activities occur across the whole life cycle in both predictive and adaptive approaches.
Business analysis removes the need for a project manager in either approach.
Business analysis is performed only on agile projects that use a backlog.
Business analysis is done only once, during predictive up-front planning.

questions.question: The PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct is organized around four core values. Which set names them correctly?
questions.explanation: The four values of the Code are responsibility, respect, fairness, and honesty. The Code organizes both aspirational and mandatory standards under these four unranked values. The other sets substitute words such as integrity, loyalty, transparency, or accountability that are not the four named values.  Takeaway: The four ethics values are responsibility, respect, fairness, and honesty.
choices: Honesty, transparency, quality, and speed.
Responsibility, respect, fairness, and honesty.
Integrity, courage, loyalty, and duty.
Responsibility, respect, accountability, and trust.

questions.question: A business analyst needs deep, detailed insight into one senior underwriter's complex decision process. Which elicitation technique fits best?
questions.explanation: An interview draws out depth and detail from an individual, which suits probing one expert's complex reasoning. A survey gathers breadth across many respondents rather than depth, and brainstorming generates new ideas instead of dissecting one person's process.  Takeaway: Use interviews for depth from an individual; use surveys for breadth across many.
choices: A review of last year's lessons-learned register.
A one-on-one interview with the senior underwriter.
A broad survey sent to the entire underwriting department.
A brainstorming session focused on generating brand-new ideas.

questions.question: A stakeholder claims that a presentation is always a one-way form of communication. Which response is most accurate?
questions.explanation: A presentation can be one-way when it simply delivers information, or interactive when it invites questions and discussion, so its type depends on the format chosen. It is not fixed as always interactive, always pull, or unusable for project information.  Takeaway: A presentation may be one-way or interactive - the format depends on whether it invites dialogue.
choices: A presentation is always pull communication because attendees choose to attend.
A presentation cannot be used to communicate any project information at all.
A presentation can be either one-way or interactive, depending on whether it invites dialogue.
A presentation is always interactive because an audience is physically present.

questions.question: A tool compares each stakeholder's current level of engagement with the level desired for project success. Which artifact is this?
questions.explanation: Comparing current engagement with the desired level is the purpose of a stakeholder engagement assessment. The stakeholder register lists who the stakeholders are and their information, but it does not chart current-versus-desired engagement.  Takeaway: Current-versus-desired engagement is an engagement assessment, not the stakeholder register.
choices: A stakeholder engagement assessment
The project charter
The stakeholder register
The project risk register

questions.question: Which statement best describes what business analysis is within a project?
questions.explanation: Business analysis is a set of activities - eliciting, analyzing, documenting, managing, and helping validate requirements - performed across the whole life cycle. It is not confined to a single early phase, and the analyst does not own value decisions or funding, which belong to the business and the sponsor.  Takeaway: Business analysis is ongoing requirement work across the life cycle, not a one-time phase or a decision authority.
choices: A single phase that is finished before the project charter is approved and signed.
The authority to decide which features will deliver the most business value.
The function that approves the project budget and authorizes all spending.
A set of activities that elicit, analyze, document, and help validate requirements throughout the life cycle.

questions.question: In a predictive project, what does the work breakdown structure (WBS) represent?
questions.explanation: The WBS is a deliverable-oriented hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work the team must carry out to meet objectives, and that scope includes project-management work, not just the product. A sequenced list of activities with dependencies is the schedule, and a chart of reporting relationships is an organizational breakdown, not a WBS. Excluding project-management work would leave the WBS short of the full authorized scope.  Takeaway: The WBS decomposes 100 percent of the authorized scope, including project-management work, not just product deliverables.
choices: A hierarchical decomposition of the total authorized scope, including project-management work
Only the physical product deliverables, deliberately excluding project-management effort
An organization chart showing the reporting relationships among team members
A sequenced list of activities with their durations and dependencies used to build the timeline

questions.question: A team is about to start a backlog item and wants to know when it will be considered successfully complete. What best defines success for that specific item?
questions.explanation: An item is successfully complete when it satisfies its acceptance criteria and the team's Definition of Done. Personal opinion, hours spent, or merely starting the item do not establish completion.  Takeaway: An item is done when it meets its acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done.
choices: When the assigned developer feels it is finished
When it is simply moved to the in-progress column
When it meets its acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done
When the maximum number of hours has been spent on it

questions.question: A project charter contains several statements. Choose the TWO that are constraints. (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Constraints are limiting factors that restrict how the project can be run, which describes both the fixed budget and the immovable go-live date. The API-readiness and compatible-device statements are taken as true without proof, making them assumptions, and a possible steel shortage is an uncertain future event, making it a risk.  Takeaway: Fixed limits on money, time, or resources are constraints.
choices: The team assumes the vendor's API will be ready by May.
The project must be completed within a $500,000 budget.
The new plant might face a steel shortage next quarter.
The go-live date is fixed at October 1 and cannot move.
Leadership assumes most users already own compatible devices.

questions.question: A key contractor has not yet confirmed whether their crew will be available during your peak construction month. How is this uncertainty best classified?
questions.explanation: Uncertainty about whether a resource will be available is a risk, because it is an uncertain condition that could affect the project. A constraint would apply only if the unavailability were already known and fixed rather than uncertain.  Takeaway: Uncertain availability is a risk; a known, fixed limit is a constraint.
choices: A risk
A milestone
A constraint
A deliverable

questions.question: On a predictive project, how are requirements typically managed after they have been approved?
questions.explanation: Predictive projects baseline requirements in a specification, maintain traceability, and route changes through a formal change control process. Continuous reprioritization without a baseline describes an adaptive approach, and 'baselined' means changes are controlled, not that requirements can never change.  Takeaway: Predictive BA uses a baselined spec plus traceability; change goes through change control.
choices: They are frozen permanently and cannot be changed under any circumstance whatsoever
They are baselined in a specification and traced, with changes handled through change control
They are continuously reprioritized in a backlog with no formal baseline maintained
They are discarded and completely re-elicited from scratch at the start of every phase

questions.question: Over several weeks a client keeps asking the team to 'just squeeze in' small features, and the team keeps agreeing without updating the baseline or using change control. What is happening?
questions.explanation: Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of scope without going through change control, which fits repeatedly adding features and skipping the baseline update. Gold-plating differs because it comes from the team adding extras rather than from the customer's requests being accepted uncontrolled.  Takeaway: Uncontrolled scope growth without change control is scope creep.
choices: Proper progressive elaboration of the plan.
Gold-plating, because extra work is being added.
Scope creep, because scope is expanding without change control.
A milestone slippage in the schedule.

questions.question: Why does a project management plan address cost, schedule, quality, risk, resources, and communications together rather than focusing on only one of them?
questions.explanation: These knowledge areas interact, so a change in one, such as scope or schedule, affects the others, and planning them together keeps the effort balanced toward its objectives. It is not a fixed regulatory template, and adding areas does not by itself shorten the schedule or make the areas independent.  Takeaway: Planning areas are interdependent and must be balanced together.
choices: Because addressing a greater number of these areas will automatically shorten the schedule.
Because each of these areas is always managed by a completely separate and independent team.
Because regulators require every project plan to contain exactly these six named sections.
Because these areas are interdependent, and managing them together keeps the project balanced toward its objectives.

questions.question: Without using any change process, a developer adds an extra animated splash screen the customer never requested because 'it looks nicer.' What is this an example of?
questions.explanation: Gold-plating occurs when the team adds features or polish the customer did not ask for, which describes the unrequested splash screen. Scope creep comes from uncontrolled changes to requested scope, and this addition originates with the team rather than from an approved change or normal elaboration.  Takeaway: When the team adds unrequested extras, that is gold-plating.
choices: An approved change to the baseline.
Gold-plating, because the team added an unrequested extra.
Scope creep introduced by the customer.
Progressive elaboration of requirements.

questions.question: In Scrum, the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers are collectively referred to using which term?
questions.explanation: Scrum defines three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers. Artifacts and phases are separate concepts, and these are not organizational departments.  Takeaway: Scrum has three accountabilities: Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers.
choices: The three artifacts of Scrum
The three accountabilities on the Scrum Team
The three departments of the company
The three phases of the sprint

questions.question: A team notes that a new tax credit MIGHT be approved next quarter, which would lower project costs if it passes. How is this best classified?
questions.explanation: A risk is a future uncertain event, and a risk with a positive effect is an opportunity, which matches a possible cost-reducing tax credit. It is not an issue because it has not occurred, and calling it an assumption would mean treating it as certain rather than uncertain.  Takeaway: An uncertain future event that could help the project is an opportunity, or positive risk.
choices: An assumption, because the team is essentially counting on the credit being approved.
An issue, because the possible credit directly involves the project's cost baseline.
A constraint, because anything that concerns the project's money acts as a limiting factor.
A risk, specifically an opportunity, because it is uncertain, in the future, and could help the project.

questions.question: The only qualified welder is already committed to another project for the first three weeks of your schedule and cannot be reassigned. How should this be treated in planning?
questions.explanation: A known, fixed limitation on the plan is a constraint, and the welder's confirmed unavailability for three weeks is exactly that. It would only be a risk if the availability were uncertain, and it is not yet an issue because nothing has gone wrong that needs escalation.  Takeaway: A known, fixed limitation is a constraint; uncertain availability is a risk.
choices: A constraint, because the unavailability is known and fixed
An issue that must be escalated immediately
An assumption to be validated during execution
A risk, because the welder might still become free

questions.question: During backlog refinement, a business analyst discovers that two candidate features address the same underlying need and recommends sequencing one ahead of the other. A teammate asks who has the authority to finalize the order of the work. What is the most accurate statement about the analyst's role?
questions.explanation: The analyst analyzes options and informs the decision by clarifying value, risk, and dependencies, but the designated product or business decision-maker (the product owner in Scrum) sets the order. Gathering the requirements does not transfer ordering authority to the analyst, and routine ordering is not a sponsor sign-off.  Takeaway: The BA informs prioritization; the designated product decision-maker owns the final order.
choices: The analyst owns the ordering decision because the analyst was the one who gathered the requirements
The analyst investigates and recommends, but the designated product decision-maker sets the final order of the work
The project sponsor must personally approve the order of every backlog item before work can proceed
The order is settled by a majority vote of the delivery team at each refinement session

questions.question: A team lead wants measures that reflect real adaptive progress and flow. Which TWO measures are appropriate for this purpose? (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Adaptive progress is best shown by working, accepted increments, and flow can be measured by cycle time from start to done. Desk hours, meeting counts, and document length do not reflect delivered value or flow.  Takeaway: Measure adaptive progress by working increments and flow metrics like cycle time, not activity counts.
choices: Working, Done increments accepted by the customer
The number of hours each person sat at a desk
Cycle time for items to move from start to done
The count of meetings attended this week
The length of the written project charter

questions.question: The 'three C's' summarize the essential aspects of a user story. From the choices below, select the TWO that are among the three C's.
questions.explanation: The three C's are Card, Conversation, and Confirmation. Of the listed choices, Card and Confirmation are correct; Contract, Compliance, and Commitment are not part of the model, and the third C, Conversation, is not among the options.  Takeaway: The three C's of a user story are Card, Conversation, and Confirmation.
choices: Card
Contract
Compliance
Confirmation
Commitment

questions.question: Users describe their daily workflow, but the analyst suspects the real steps differ from what people report. Which technique best reveals what users actually do?
questions.explanation: Observation or job shadowing reveals reality versus what people say, so it exposes the true steps when reported and actual behavior may differ. Asking again through a questionnaire just repeats the stated version, and brainstorming imagines an ideal rather than capturing current practice.  Takeaway: Use observation or job shadowing to see real behavior versus what people say they do.
choices: Observation or job shadowing of users doing the actual work.
A document review of the outdated process manual.
A brainstorming session to imagine an ideal future workflow.
A questionnaire asking users to describe their workflow once more.

questions.question: In an adaptive project, how is detailed scope for upcoming work primarily developed and kept current?
questions.explanation: Adaptive scope is elaborated progressively through ongoing backlog refinement, adding detail to items as they near development. Fully detailing or freezing everything up front contradicts the adaptive intent to respond to learning.  Takeaway: Adaptive scope is elaborated progressively through continuous backlog refinement.
choices: By letting only the project sponsor write each item in full
By freezing the backlog after the first planning session
By fully detailing every requirement before any work begins
Through ongoing backlog refinement as understanding grows

questions.question: A product fully meets its written specifications, but it was intentionally built with a limited feature set to keep costs down. How is this product best characterized?
questions.explanation: Quality is the degree to which the product fulfills its requirements and is fit for use, so a product that fully meets its specifications is high quality regardless of how many features it has. Grade is a category based on features or technical characteristics, so a deliberately limited feature set is low grade. Mixing these up, or treating fewer features as automatically low quality, confuses two distinct concepts.  Takeaway: Quality means meeting requirements and fitness for use; grade is a feature category. A product can be high quality and low grade.
choices: High quality but low grade, since it meets requirements yet offers fewer features
Low quality and low grade, because it deliberately offers only a few features
High quality and high grade, because it fully meets its written specifications
Low quality but high grade, because fewer features somehow mean higher performance

questions.question: A stakeholder claims the product backlog and the requirements traceability matrix (RTM) are the same thing under different names. Which statement best corrects this?
questions.explanation: An RTM records explicit trace links from origin through design, build, and test to show coverage, whereas a product backlog is the ordered list of work in adaptive delivery. They are related but not a one-to-one substitute, and neither is a fixed-date schedule.  Takeaway: RTM tracks trace links for coverage; the product backlog orders adaptive work. Related, not identical.
choices: Both are fixed-date schedules and can therefore be used interchangeably on any project
The backlog records origin-to-test trace links, while the RTM orders the adaptive work
They are identical; the RTM is simply the predictive name for a product backlog
The RTM records trace links for coverage, while the backlog is the ordered list of adaptive work

questions.question: Match each spending example to its cost-of-quality category.
questions.explanation: Cost of quality splits into conformance and nonconformance spending. Prevention (building quality in, like mistake-proofing) and appraisal (inspecting and testing) are conformance costs incurred to avoid defects. Internal failure (defects caught before delivery) and external failure (defects reaching the customer) are nonconformance costs; external failures are the most expensive because they reach the customer.  Takeaway: Prevention and appraisal are conformance costs paid to avoid defects; internal and external failures are the costlier price of nonconformance.
pairs: Adding mistake-proofing to the assembly line before production starts
Prevention costs
Inspecting and testing finished units before release
Appraisal costs
Scrapping a defective batch caught during in-house testing
Internal failure costs
Reimbursing customers for a defect discovered after delivery
External failure costs

questions.question: A team is moving from a predictive mindset to an adaptive one. In predictive planning the scope was decomposed into a work breakdown structure. What is the closest adaptive equivalent used to organize and order the work?
questions.explanation: In adaptive work the product backlog is the ordered list of items that captures and organizes scope, similar in purpose to how a work breakdown structure organizes predictive scope. A Gantt chart and change log are predictive control tools, and a risk register tracks risks, not scope.  Takeaway: The product backlog is the adaptive counterpart to a WBS for organizing scope.
choices: A risk register of threats only
A prioritized product backlog of items
A fixed Gantt chart of every task
A signed change control log

questions.question: A project has stable, well-understood requirements and a fixed regulatory design that is very unlikely to change. Which development approach fits best?
questions.explanation: A predictive, plan-based approach suits work where requirements are clear and stable early, letting scope, schedule, and cost be defined up front. Adaptive approaches are chosen when requirements change often, which is the opposite of this stable situation.  Takeaway: Stable, well-defined requirements favor a predictive approach.
choices: Adaptive, because stable requirements need frequent iterations.
Incremental, because a fixed design must ship in small slices.
Extreme, because regulations are involved.
Predictive, because the scope can be defined up front and change is minimal.

questions.question: A team releases a working login feature, then in the next cycle adds a working search feature, and later adds a working checkout feature, each usable on its own. This approach is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery adds new, usable pieces of the product over time. Repeatedly improving one deliverable is iterative, and a single end delivery is a big-bang predictive release.  Takeaway: Incremental delivery adds usable slices; each increment provides value on its own.
choices: Iterative refinement of one feature over time
Incremental delivery of usable slices
Refactoring the same feature repeatedly
A big-bang delivery at project end

questions.question: Which Scrum event exists mainly to help the team improve how it works together?
questions.explanation: The Sprint Retrospective focuses on inspecting how the team worked and planning improvements. Sprint Planning sets up the Sprint, and the Review inspects the product increment.  Takeaway: The Retrospective is where the team improves how it works.
choices: Sprint Planning
The Daily Scrum
The Sprint Retrospective
The Sprint Review

questions.question: Match each schedule dependency term to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Finish-to-Start is the most common relationship: the successor waits for the predecessor to finish. Start-to-Start lets the successor begin once the predecessor has begun. A lead accelerates the successor, letting it start before the predecessor finishes, while a lag inserts deliberate waiting time. Confusing leads (acceleration) with lags (delay) is the usual error.  Takeaway: Leads pull a successor earlier; lags push it later; FS and SS describe which predecessor event releases the successor.
pairs: Finish-to-Start (FS)
The successor cannot begin until the predecessor finishes
Start-to-Start (SS)
The successor cannot begin until the predecessor begins
Lead
The successor is allowed to start before the predecessor finishes
Lag
An imposed waiting period is inserted between predecessor and successor

questions.question: What is the primary reason an organization groups related projects into a program instead of running each one independently?
questions.explanation: Programs exist to deliver benefits and control that would not be available if the related projects were managed on their own. Shared end dates and identical budgets are not the defining purpose, and programs typically exist precisely because the projects do have dependencies worth coordinating.  Takeaway: Programs deliver coordinated benefits beyond what individual projects can achieve alone.
choices: To make certain the related projects end up having no dependencies on one another.
To gain benefits and coordinated control not available from managing the projects separately.
To require all of the related projects to draw funding from one single identical budget.
To force every one of the related projects to finish on exactly the same calendar date.

questions.question: On a predictive project, a stakeholder submits a formal change request that would expand the scope. What should the project manager do?
questions.explanation: Changes on a predictive project follow the change management plan: the request is evaluated for its impact, a decision to approve or reject is made through the defined authority, and baselines are updated only after approval. Implementing immediately bypasses that control. Baselines are approved and controlled, not permanently frozen, so refusing all change is wrong, and updating the baseline before approval reverses the required order.  Takeaway: Evaluate the change, get it approved, then update baselines; never change baselines before approval.
choices: Reject the request outright because project baselines are frozen once they have been set
Implement the requested change right away so that the key stakeholder stays fully satisfied
Update the scope baseline first and then seek approval for the change
Evaluate the request through change control and update baselines only after it is approved

questions.question: Which statement best explains how a project acts as a vehicle for change?
questions.explanation: A project drives change by transitioning an organization from its current state to a desired future state through the outputs it delivers, which then enable new capabilities and benefits. It does not leave operations unchanged, guarantee strategic success, or eliminate the ongoing operations that sustain the new capability.  Takeaway: Projects move an organization from a current state to a desired future state.
choices: It provides an organization with an absolute guarantee that its overall strategy is definitely going to succeed.
It moves the organization from its current state to a desired future state, delivering outputs that enable new benefits.
It permanently removes the need for any kind of ongoing operational work once the whole project has been finished.
It keeps the organization's existing operations exactly as they are while merely producing routine status reports.

questions.question: A project reports PV = 50,000, EV = 44,000, and AC = 40,000. Which statement best describes its overall status?
questions.explanation: Schedule variance = EV - PV = 44,000 - 50,000 = -6,000, and a negative schedule variance means the project is behind schedule. Cost variance = EV - AC = 44,000 - 40,000 = +4,000, and a positive cost variance means the project is under budget. So the project is behind schedule and under budget, which is why the combinations claiming ahead of schedule or over budget are incorrect.  Takeaway: Compute SV = EV - PV and CV = EV - AC separately; negative SV is behind schedule, positive CV is under budget.
choices: Ahead of schedule and under budget
Ahead of schedule and over budget
Behind schedule and under budget
Behind schedule and over budget

questions.question: Match each estimating technique to the situation where it fits best.
questions.explanation: Analogous estimating is top-down and quick, using a similar project's actuals when detail is scarce. Parametric estimating applies a statistical unit rate, so it needs a reliable relationship like cost per unit. Three-point estimating tackles uncertainty by weighting optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values. Bottom-up estimating is the most accurate but needs a fully decomposed scope.  Takeaway: Match the estimating technique to the data available: analogous when detail is thin, parametric when a unit rate exists, three-point for uncertainty, bottom-up when scope is decomposed.
pairs: Analogous estimating
Very early planning with little detail, scaling from a similar past project's actuals
Parametric estimating
A reliable unit rate exists, such as cost per square metre, to calculate the estimate
Three-point (PERT) estimating
High uncertainty, so optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic values are averaged
Bottom-up estimating
The scope is fully decomposed, so each work package is estimated and the results summed

questions.question: By the end of a Sprint, the Developers completed the most important items and met the Sprint Goal, but two low-priority items remain unfinished. How should this outcome be viewed?
questions.explanation: The Sprint Goal is the commitment for the Sprint, so achieving it means the Sprint met its purpose even if minor items carry over. The Sprint is not defined as finishing every backlog item, and Sprints are not extended.  Takeaway: The Sprint Goal is the commitment, not completing every backlog item.
choices: The Sprint Goal is irrelevant if any item is incomplete
The Sprint met its commitment because the Sprint Goal was achieved
The team must extend the Sprint until all items are done
The Sprint failed because not every item was finished

questions.question: Choose TWO of the following that are best classified as operations rather than projects. (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Operations are the ongoing, repetitive activities that keep the business running, which describes recurring payroll cycles and the day-to-day help desk. The portal build, the data-center migration, and the logo rebrand are each temporary efforts producing a unique result, so they are projects, not operations.  Takeaway: Repetitive, sustaining work is operations; temporary unique efforts are projects.
choices: Processing employee payroll on the same cycle every two weeks.
Building a brand-new customer portal to launch next spring.
Migrating the data center to a new provider by year-end.
Running the company help desk day to day on an ongoing basis.
Designing a one-time rebrand of the corporate logo.

questions.question: Arrange the steps of building a predictive project budget in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Budgeting rolls costs upward: activity estimates aggregate into work packages and control accounts, then contingency reserves for identified risks are added to create the cost baseline. Management reserves for unforeseen risks sit outside the baseline and are added last to reach the total project budget. Contingency is inside the baseline; management reserve is not.  Takeaway: The cost baseline includes contingency reserves; adding management reserves on top yields the total project budget.
sequence: Estimate the cost of each individual activity
Aggregate activity costs into work-package and control-account costs
Add contingency reserves to form the cost baseline
Add management reserves on top of the cost baseline to set the total budget

questions.question: A project runs under a fixed-price contract in a regulated industry. A team member insists this automatically requires a fully predictive approach. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Contract type and regulatory setting influence controls and documentation but do not by themselves dictate the development approach; suitability turns on how stable and well understood the requirements are and how much change is expected. Adaptive or hybrid delivery can be used in fixed-price or regulated contexts with appropriate governance. Claims that fixed-price always requires predictive, or that regulation always requires adaptive, both overstate a single factor.  Takeaway: Fixed-price and regulated settings do not auto-require predictive; suitability depends on requirement stability and expected change.
choices: Agree; regulated industries legally prohibit any adaptive or iterative delivery methods
Agree; a fixed-price contract removes all scope uncertainty, so a predictive approach is mandatory
Disagree, but only because regulated projects must always be adaptive to satisfy auditors
Disagree; the approach depends on requirement stability and expected change, not the contract type alone

questions.question: A candidate wants to know how much of the current CAPM exam covers Business Analysis and how that weight compares with the other domains. Which statement is accurate?
questions.explanation: Business Analysis carries about 27 percent of the exam, which makes it the second-largest domain behind the roughly 36 percent Project Management Fundamentals domain. Calling it the largest is wrong because Fundamentals is bigger, and its weight is not defined as the predictive and agile content added together.  Takeaway: Business Analysis is 27 percent of CAPM - the second-largest domain, behind Fundamentals.
choices: About 27 percent - the second-largest domain, behind Project Management Fundamentals.
It is weighted the same as the predictive and agile content combined.
It is a minor topic that surfaces in only a handful of scattered items.
It is the largest domain, at roughly 36 percent of the total exam.

questions.question: On an adaptive project, a new insight from a customer demo suggests a higher-value capability than the one planned next. How is this typically handled?
questions.explanation: Adaptive delivery expects the backlog to be continuously refined and reprioritized as new information arrives, with the designated decision-maker resetting the order. Routing normal reprioritization through formal change control or freezing the backlog reflects predictive change handling, not adaptive practice.  Takeaway: Adaptive BA continuously refines and reprioritizes the backlog rather than using formal change control.
choices: Refine the backlog and let the designated decision-maker reprioritize the upcoming work
Submit a formal change request through the change control board before making any adjustment
Reject the insight outright because the requirements were already agreed and signed off
Freeze the current backlog order until the next scheduled baseline review takes place

questions.question: Requirements for a new consumer app are expected to change often as the market is explored, and stakeholders want working features early and frequently. Which approach is most appropriate, and why?
questions.explanation: An adaptive approach is chosen when requirements are volatile and stakeholders want frequent, incremental value, both of which describe this app. Predictive and waterfall approaches lock scope early and are ill-suited to requirements expected to change often.  Takeaway: High change plus a need for frequent value points to an adaptive approach.
choices: Adaptive, because it welcomes changing requirements and delivers value in short cycles.
Predictive, because delivering the early features first would require a completely fixed baseline.
Predictive, because a detailed up-front plan will prevent the requirements from changing.
Waterfall, because running sequential phases will deliver the finished app faster to market.

questions.question: Which statement about process groups is accurate?
questions.explanation: Process groups are logical groupings of project-management activities, not project phases. They overlap and recur across the life of a project or a single phase, so planning, executing, and monitoring and controlling happen repeatedly and concurrently. Treating them as one-time sequential phases, or claiming executing must end before monitoring begins, misrepresents how the activities actually interact.  Takeaway: Process groups are overlapping, recurring activity categories, not sequential project phases.
choices: Process groups are categories of activities that overlap and can recur throughout a project or phase
Executing must be fully finished before any Monitoring and Controlling work can begin
Each process group executes exactly once and never repeats during the project
Process groups are the sequential life-cycle phases a project passes through once, in a fixed order

questions.question: A project's critical path is 20 days. A non-critical activity that has 4 days of total float is delayed by 6 days. All else being equal, what happens to the project finish?
questions.explanation: The activity can absorb up to its 4 days of total float with no effect on the finish date. The 6-day delay exceeds that float by 6 - 4 = 2 days, so the project finish slips by 2 days to 22 days. Assuming no change ignores that the delay is larger than the float. Adding the full 6 days ignores the float entirely, and adding 4 days mistakes the amount of float for the amount of slip.  Takeaway: A non-critical activity delays the project only by the amount its delay exceeds its total float.
choices: Delayed by 4 days; the project now finishes in 24 days
No change; the project still finishes in 20 days
Delayed by 2 days; the project now finishes in 22 days
Delayed by 6 days; the project now finishes in 26 days

questions.question: During project closure, a new project manager prepares to conduct formal procurement closure. The project used only internal staff and made no external purchases. What is the appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Procurement closure applies only where procurements actually exist; with no external contracts, there is nothing to close and the step is simply omitted. Performing it anyway, seeking a waiver, or creating a procurement solely to close it would all add pointless effort.  Takeaway: Close procurements only when procurements were actually made.
choices: Skip procurement closure because no procurements were made
Conduct procurement closure anyway just to be thorough
Escalate to the contracts department to obtain a waiver
Delay closure until a procurement can be created

questions.question: A stakeholder believes the Sprint Review is a formal gate where they must approve or reject the project before work may continue. How should this be corrected?
questions.explanation: The Sprint Review is a collaborative session to inspect the increment and adapt the Product Backlog, not a formal approval gate. It is not a one-way status report, and it does not replace the other events.  Takeaway: The Sprint Review inspects the increment and adapts the backlog; it is not a sign-off gate.
choices: They are right; no work continues without their signature
The Sprint Review is only for the Scrum Master to report status
The Sprint Review is a working session to inspect the increment and adapt the Product Backlog together
The Sprint Review replaces all of the other Scrum events

questions.question: On a predictive project, which pairing correctly separates the sponsor's role from the project manager's role?
questions.explanation: The sponsor funds and champions the project, while the project manager delivers it. Having the sponsor manage daily work reverses the roles, and the sponsor does not author requirements nor share an identical role with the project manager.  Takeaway: The sponsor funds and champions; the project manager delivers.
choices: The sponsor manages the day-to-day work; the project manager provides the funding.
The sponsor and the project manager share identical responsibilities on the project.
The sponsor provides funding and business backing; the project manager delivers the project.
The sponsor writes the requirements; the project manager approves the budget.

questions.question: A business analyst wants to reduce the risk of building the wrong thing before significant development effort is spent. Which approach best validates requirements early?
questions.explanation: Early validation uses prototypes and demos with real users to confirm the solution meets the actual need before heavy investment. Waiting until final release validates too late, and a signed document or more spec-based tests only confirms conformance to the spec (verification), not the real need.  Takeaway: Validate early with prototypes and demos against the real need, not just the spec.
choices: Rely solely on the signed requirements document as sufficient proof of correctness
Increase the number of internal test cases run against the written specification
Put prototypes or demos in front of real users to confirm the requirements meet the real need
Wait until the final release is complete before confirming the solution with any users

questions.question: A team performs an audit of the processes used to produce deliverables, confirming the correct procedures are being followed. This activity is an example of what?
questions.explanation: Quality assurance is process-focused: it audits and improves the processes and standards used to produce work, which is exactly what a process audit does. Quality control, by contrast, inspects the outputs or deliverables themselves to verify they meet requirements, so both the inspection and the measurement descriptions point to control, not assurance. Validate Scope concerns customer acceptance, which is a different activity entirely.  Takeaway: Quality assurance audits the process; quality control inspects the output.
choices: Quality assurance, because it audits the processes used to create the deliverables
Quality control, because a finished deliverable is being inspected closely for defects
Validate Scope, because the customer is formally accepting deliverables
Control Quality, because measurements of the output are being recorded

questions.question: Who is generally in the best position to provide effort estimates for the activities they will perform?
questions.explanation: The people who will actually perform the activities understand them best and are therefore best placed to estimate the effort involved. The sponsor, an auditor, and a legal department are removed from the hands-on work and lack that direct insight.  Takeaway: Those doing the work are best placed to estimate it.
choices: The customer's legal department
The external quality auditor
The project sponsor who funds the project
The team members who will do the work

questions.question: Which responsibility most clearly belongs to the project sponsor?
questions.explanation: The sponsor provides the funding and authorizes the project by signing the charter. Breaking down tasks, running tests, and estimating effort are carried out by the team who perform the work, not by the sponsor.  Takeaway: The sponsor funds the project and authorizes the charter.
choices: Producing the detailed breakdown of project tasks
Writing and running the daily test scripts
Providing funding and authorizing the project charter
Estimating the effort for each activity

questions.question: An associate insists that predictive and waterfall mean exactly the same thing. Which correction is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Predictive is the broad plan-based category, and waterfall is one sequential way of carrying out a predictive project, so waterfall is a subset of predictive. Treating them as opposites or labeling waterfall adaptive misstates both terms.  Takeaway: Waterfall is a type of predictive; predictive is the wider category.
choices: They are opposites, because predictive welcomes change and waterfall forbids it.
Waterfall is one sequential pattern within the broader predictive, plan-based category.
Predictive is one specific type of waterfall approach.
Waterfall is an adaptive approach, while predictive is plan-based.

questions.question: Arrange the steps of the lessons-learned process in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Knowledge management delivers value only when lessons flow through the full cycle: teams identify a lesson during the work, record it in the project's lessons-learned register, then analyze and move it into the organization's repository so it outlives the project. The final and often-skipped step is retrieving and applying it on later work.  Takeaway: A lesson delivers value only when it is identified, documented, stored organization-wide, and then actually reused.
sequence: Identify the lesson as work is performed and outcomes become clear
Document the lesson in the project's lessons-learned register
Analyze and finalize the lesson, then store it in the organization's lessons-learned repository
Retrieve and apply the lesson on current and future projects

questions.question: A team debates the difference between acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done. Which statement is accurate?
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are specific to a single item, while the Definition of Done is a broader shared standard the increment must meet. The Definition of Done is prominent in Scrum but is not exclusive to any one framework.  Takeaway: Acceptance criteria are per item; the Definition of Done is a broader quality standard.
choices: The Definition of Done is used only in Kanban and never in Scrum
Acceptance criteria apply to the whole product, while the Definition of Done is unique to one item
Acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done are the same checklist
Acceptance criteria are item-specific, while the Definition of Done is a broader quality standard for the increment

questions.question: A team member says an activity will take five days of work. Because a holiday weekend falls in the middle, those five work days stretch across nine calendar days. What value should be recorded as the activity's duration?
questions.explanation: Duration is the number of work periods required to complete an activity, independent of how nonworking days spread it across the calendar; five work periods remain five regardless of the holiday. Counting the calendar span confuses duration with elapsed calendar time, and duration can be estimated without waiting for the final calendar.  Takeaway: Duration counts work periods, not the calendar days they span.
choices: 7, as a compromise between work and calendar days
9, because that reflects the calendar span including nonworking days
5, because duration counts the required work periods
The duration cannot be set until the full calendar is finalized

questions.question: A delivered feature passes every test against its written specification, yet during a demo real users say it does not actually solve their problem. In verification-and-validation terms, what happened?
questions.explanation: Verification confirms the solution was built to the specification, which the passing tests show, while validation confirms it meets the real need, which the user feedback shows it does not. The two are distinct activities, so passing one while failing the other is entirely possible.  Takeaway: Verify means built to spec; validate means it meets the real need. They can disagree.
choices: Verification and validation mean the same thing, so the described result is self-contradictory
The feature was verified against the spec but was not validated against users' real need
The feature failed verification against the spec but nonetheless passed validation with users
Both verification and validation clearly succeeded, so the negative user feedback is a mistake

questions.question: A team wants a simple chart that shows how much work remains in the current iteration as the days pass. Which chart best serves this purpose?
questions.explanation: A burndown chart tracks remaining work trending down over the iteration. A burnup chart shows completed work against a scope line, and a cumulative flow diagram shows how items move through states.  Takeaway: Burndown shows work remaining; burnup shows work completed.
choices: A stakeholder register of contacts
A burnup chart of completed work
A cumulative flow diagram of states
A burndown chart of remaining work

questions.question: Which set of practices is most associated with Extreme Programming (XP)?
questions.explanation: Extreme Programming centers on engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, and small releases. Formal gates and heavy up-front documentation are more characteristic of plan-driven, predictive settings, though predictive work does not mandate either in every case.  Takeaway: XP is defined by engineering practices like pairing, TDD, and continuous integration.
choices: Fixed change control boards and formal sign-off gates
Detailed up-front documentation before any code is written
Pair programming, test-driven development, and continuous integration
A single delivery at the very end of the project

questions.question: A quality reviewer confirms that a finished pump matches every measurement on its approved design drawings. Which activity is this, and what question does it answer?
questions.explanation: Verification checks the product against its specification, asking 'did we build it right?'—exactly what confirming the pump against its drawings does. Validation asks 'did we build the right thing?' by testing against the customer's real need. Options that pair verification with customer satisfaction, or validation with specification conformance, swap the two definitions.  Takeaway: Verification checks conformance to the specification; validation checks fitness for the customer's actual need.
choices: Validation, which answers whether the product conforms to its written specification
Validation, which answers whether the product meets the customer's actual need
Verification, which answers whether the product was built to its specification
Verification, which answers whether the customer is satisfied with the outcome

questions.question: A risk that the team had identified and rated has now actually occurred. What has it become?
questions.explanation: A risk is an uncertain event; once it actually occurs, that uncertainty is gone and it becomes an issue that must now be managed. It does not turn into a constraint or an assumption, which are different planning concepts.  Takeaway: A risk that materializes becomes an issue to be managed.
choices: A milestone
An issue
An assumption
A constraint

questions.question: Which organizational condition tends to make sustaining an adaptive approach more difficult?
questions.explanation: Adaptive delivery depends on fast feedback and the ability to change direction, so rigid silos and lengthy approval chains slow it down. Empowered cross-functional teams and easy access to a business voice support adaptive work.  Takeaway: Rigid silos and slow approvals work against adaptive delivery.
choices: A culture that accepts learning through short feedback loops
Siloed hand-offs requiring long formal approvals to change work
Small cross-functional teams empowered to decide
Regular access to a business representative for feedback

questions.question: Arrange the steps a project manager should take to respond to a schedule slippage in the correct order.
questions.explanation: Schedule compression starts by confirming the delay against the baseline, then focusing only on the critical path, since off-path work does not move the finish date. Fast-tracking (overlapping activities, adding risk) and crashing (adding resources, adding cost) are alternatives evaluated together - neither must be tried first - and the option with the least negative impact is chosen and the plan updated through change control rather than informally.  Takeaway: Compress only the critical path, weigh fast-tracking's risk against crashing's cost as alternatives, and rebaseline through change control.
sequence: Confirm the schedule is truly behind by comparing status against the schedule baseline
Identify which activities lie on the critical path
Evaluate the schedule-compression options - fast-tracking (overlap activities, adds risk) and crashing (add resources, adds cost)
Select the compression option with the least negative impact and update the plan through change control

questions.question: A project builds its fixed hardware platform on a predictive schedule while developing the companion mobile app in short adaptive sprints. What approach is being used?
questions.explanation: A hybrid approach deliberately combines predictive and adaptive methods within the same project, which fits scheduling the hardware predictively while developing the app in sprints. Labeling it purely adaptive or purely predictive ignores that both styles are in use at once.  Takeaway: Mixing predictive and adaptive on one project is a hybrid approach.
choices: Hybrid, because it combines predictive and adaptive elements on one project.
Purely predictive, because a schedule exists.
Iterative only, because the app is refined in cycles.
Purely adaptive, because sprints are involved.

questions.question: On a Scrum Team, who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog and deciding the priority of value?
questions.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog and deciding what is most valuable. The Scrum Master supports the process rather than assigning items, and the Developers decide how much to pull, not the backlog order.  Takeaway: The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog and owns value priority.
choices: The Product Owner
The Developers, who vote on every item
The Scrum Master, who assigns each item
The functional manager outside the team

questions.question: In a WBS, a work package is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: A work package is the work at the lowest level of the WBS, small enough that its cost and duration can be reliably estimated and its progress managed. The topmost element is the overall project or major deliverable, not a work package. Sequenced activities belong to the schedule, and a milestone is a zero-duration event rather than a package of work.  Takeaway: A work package is the lowest-level WBS component where cost and duration are estimated.
choices: The single topmost element that represents the final overall deliverable of the whole project effort
The work at the lowest level of the WBS, where cost and duration can be estimated and managed
A grouping of related activities already sequenced in the project schedule
A milestone that marks the completion of a project phase

questions.question: A startup is developing a consumer app in a fast-moving market where user needs are expected to change many times before launch. Which condition most strongly favors an adaptive approach over a predictive one?
questions.explanation: Adaptive approaches fit high uncertainty where requirements evolve, letting the plan change as the team learns. Fixed scope with change blocked and routine, well-understood work both point toward a predictive approach.  Takeaway: Choose adaptive when uncertainty is high and change is expected; choose predictive when scope is stable and well understood.
choices: A single large release is required only at the very end
The full scope is fixed and approvals block any change
The work is routine and has been repeated many times before
Requirements are volatile and expected to change often

questions.question: Midway through a facilities upgrade, another department repeatedly refuses to release a specialist the project needs, and the project manager's own attempts to negotiate have failed, stalling the work. What is the project manager's most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: The sponsor champions the project and holds organizational authority the project manager lacks, so escalating a cross-department resource blocker the PM cannot resolve is appropriate. Silently absorbing the delay hides a real impediment; a change request cannot compel another department to act; and reassigning specialist work to untrained members risks quality and schedule.  Takeaway: When a blocker exceeds the project manager's authority, escalate to the sponsor, who can remove organizational obstacles.
choices: Escalate to the sponsor, whose authority can help remove the cross-department blocker
Reassign the specialist's tasks to existing team members to keep the work moving
Issue a formal change request instructing the other department to release the specialist immediately
Absorb the delay and re-plan the schedule around the missing specialist without raising the issue

questions.question: Before planning communications on a new benefits-enrollment system, a business analyst maps each stakeholder's influence and interest. How should this analysis shape the communication approach?
questions.explanation: Stakeholder analysis tailors communication: high-influence, high-interest stakeholders need frequent, detailed engagement, while low-interest stakeholders need only lightweight updates. Sending everyone identical reports buries key stakeholders in noise; concentrating on the powerful alone ignores others who can still affect the outcome; and delaying communication until sign-off forfeits valuable early engagement.  Takeaway: Use stakeholder analysis to match each stakeholder's communication frequency and depth to their influence and interest.
choices: Concentrate communication on the highest-influence stakeholders and give the rest minimal attention
Delay all communication until the requirements are fully signed off
Send all stakeholders the same detailed report so everyone receives identical information
Tailor communication frequency and detail to each stakeholder's influence and interest

questions.question: Activity M has an Early Finish (EF) of day 10. Its only successor, activity N, has an Early Start (ES) of day 14 (day-numbering where free float = min(ES of successors) - EF - 1). What is the free float of activity M?
questions.explanation: Free float = min(ES of successors) - EF - 1 = 14 - 10 - 1 = 3 days. This is how long M can slip without delaying the early start of its successor N. Getting 4 days comes from omitting the -1 day adjustment used in this numbering, and 0 days would assume there is no gap between M finishing and N starting, which the dates contradict.  Takeaway: Free float = earliest successor ES minus this activity's EF minus 1; it protects the successor's early start.
choices: 4 days
3 days
0 days
2 days

questions.question: A team member realizes a status report they already sent contained an error that made progress look better than it truly is. What does the Code of Ethics direct them to do?
questions.explanation: Honesty requires providing accurate information in a timely manner and correcting errors, so the credited action is to disclose and fix the misstatement. Waiting, hiding the correction, or shifting blame all conflict with the duty to be truthful and to take responsibility.  Takeaway: When you find an error, disclose it and correct it promptly.
choices: Promptly correct the report and disclose the true status to affected stakeholders.
Ask a colleague to take responsibility for the mistake.
Quietly fix it in the next report without mentioning the error.
Wait to see whether anyone notices before saying anything.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a milestone from an activity in a predictive schedule?
questions.explanation: A milestone marks a significant point or event, such as a phase completion or an approval, and carries zero duration. An activity is a distinct scheduled component of work that does consume time and resources. Milestones do not have duration, so descriptions that give them the longest duration or the most resource consumption reverse the definitions.  Takeaway: Milestones are zero-duration events; activities are work that consumes time and resources.
choices: An activity carries zero duration, while a milestone is what consumes the most time and resources on the project
A milestone and an activity are simply two names for the same schedule element
A milestone is a zero-duration point or event; an activity is scheduled work that consumes time and resources
A milestone always has the longest duration of any item on the schedule

questions.question: Stakeholders ask the team for a product roadmap. Which statement best describes what a roadmap is meant to communicate?
questions.explanation: A roadmap communicates direction over time through goals, themes, and approximate timing rather than firm delivery dates. A baselined specification and the ordered pull-list (the product backlog) are different artifacts that serve different purposes.  Takeaway: A roadmap shows direction and intent over time, not a committed fixed-date schedule.
choices: A detailed requirements specification that has been baselined for change control
The intended direction over time, showing goals, themes, and rough timing
The ordered list of work items the team pulls from during each iteration
A fixed-date schedule committing each feature to an exact delivery day

questions.question: Midway through a release, the Product Owner reorders the product backlog so a newly urgent item rises to the top for the next iteration. How should this reordering be treated?
questions.explanation: Reprioritizing and reordering the backlog is normal, expected work in an adaptive approach and does not trigger formal change control. It is not a planning failure or a baseline breach requiring sign-off.  Takeaway: Reordering the backlog is routine adaptive work, not formal change control.
choices: As a scope baseline breach needing sponsor sign-off
As a formal change request requiring a change control board
As a failure of the original planning effort
As routine backlog management, not formal change control

questions.question: During Sprint Planning, who selects how many Product Backlog items to bring into the Sprint and owns the resulting Sprint Backlog?
questions.explanation: The Developers select the items they can complete and own the Sprint Backlog, adhering to the Definition of Done. The Product Owner clarifies priority and value but does not decide the amount, and the Scrum Master facilitates rather than fills the Sprint.  Takeaway: Developers select Sprint items and own the Sprint Backlog.
choices: The Product Owner alone decides the amount
The sponsor sets the Sprint scope
The Scrum Master fills the Sprint for the team
The Developers select the items and own the Sprint Backlog

questions.question: A business analyst draws a diagram showing the new payroll system in the center, with the external users, departments, and systems that exchange data with it arranged around the edges. What does this context diagram primarily communicate?
questions.explanation: A context diagram places the solution at the center and shows the external entities and systems that exchange data with it, defining the solution's scope boundary—what is inside versus outside. It deliberately hides internal design and process detail, so options describing step-by-step flows, schedules, or internal tables mistake it for other models.  Takeaway: A context diagram frames solution scope by showing the boundary between the solution and the external entities it interacts with.
choices: The scope boundary of the solution and what lies inside versus outside it
The detailed sequence of steps a user follows to complete a task
The internal database tables and code modules of the payroll system
The project schedule and the order in which features will be delivered

questions.question: Two departments strongly disagree about a requirement, and emotions are running high. Which communication method best fits resolving this nuanced, sensitive negotiation?
questions.explanation: Interactive communication such as a conversation or workshop is best for sensitive, nuanced, or negotiation situations because it allows real-time give and take. Push and pull methods send or store information but cannot support the back-and-forth needed to work through conflict.  Takeaway: Use interactive communication for sensitive, nuanced, or negotiation situations.
choices: Push communication, such as a mass email sent to all staff.
Interactive communication, such as a facilitated conversation or workshop.
Pull communication, such as posting a document to a shared wiki.
A one-way status report distributed to the executive team.

questions.question: A newly identified risk is assigned an owner. Which statement about the risk owner is correct?
questions.explanation: A risk owner is the individual best placed to watch for the risk and carry out its response, which is not automatically the project manager, the sponsor, or the person who identified it. Ownership follows capability to act, not role or who spotted the risk.  Takeaway: A risk owner is whoever can best monitor and respond, not automatically the PM.
choices: The person best positioned to monitor and respond to the risk owns it
The person who first identified the risk always owns it
The sponsor must personally own all high-priority risks
The project manager automatically owns every risk on the project

questions.question: A hospital installs a new scheduling system. Afterward patients experience shorter wait times, and over the year the hospital gains higher patient satisfaction and revenue. Which mapping to output, outcome, and benefit is correct?
questions.explanation: The output is the deliverable produced (the system), the outcome is the change it enables (shorter waits), and the benefit is the realized value (higher satisfaction and revenue). The other mappings swap the deliverable, the change, and the value out of their correct order.  Takeaway: Output (deliverable) leads to outcome (change) leads to benefit (value).
choices: The system is the output, the shorter waits are the outcome, and the higher satisfaction and revenue are the benefit.
The system is the outcome, the revenue is the output, and the shorter waits are the benefit.
The shorter waits are the output, the system is the outcome, and satisfaction is the benefit.
The system is the benefit, the shorter waits are the output, and the revenue is the outcome.

questions.question: When should stakeholder identification take place on a project?
questions.explanation: Stakeholder identification is continuous because new stakeholders can appear at any point in the life cycle. Treating it as a one-time initiation task, or waiting until requirements are baselined or someone complains, leaves people and their needs undiscovered.  Takeaway: Stakeholder identification is continuous, not a one-time initiation step.
choices: Only once, during initiation, and never revisited afterward.
Continuously throughout the project, because new stakeholders can emerge at any time.
Only after the project requirements have been baselined.
Only when a stakeholder complains about being left out.

questions.question: A builder is constructing the 40th house in a subdivision using the exact standard floor plan it has used 39 times. A trainee says this cannot be a project because it is repetitive. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Temporary and unique refer to the endeavor and its result, not to whether the design has been used before, so each individually delivered house is a project even with a standardized plan. Repetition of a plan does not convert distinct, one-time builds into ongoing operations, and a portfolio or program describes groupings rather than a single house build.  Takeaway: A repeated design still yields unique projects; uniqueness is in the result, not the novelty of the plan.
choices: The trainee is correct; reusing the very same floor plan turns these repeated house builds into ongoing operations.
It is a portfolio, because the many houses are grouped and jointly managed together across the whole subdivision.
It is a program, because the 40 houses are related components that all happen to share one common standard design.
It is still a project; each house is a temporary effort producing a unique result on its own lot, with its own buyer and permits.

questions.question: An associate reviewing a scope statement notices it lists deliverables but never states what is explicitly out of scope. Why does this matter?
questions.explanation: Documenting what is out of scope clarifies boundaries and reduces the misunderstandings that fuel scope creep, so a missing exclusions section is a real gap. Exclusions are useful across approaches and are not what authorizes a charter or turns a document into a contract.  Takeaway: Naming exclusions guards the boundary against scope creep.
choices: Exclusions are only ever needed on adaptive projects, and are not required on predictive ones.
Without a written list of exclusions, the project charter simply cannot be formally signed.
Exclusions are the element that turns an ordinary scope statement into a binding legal contract.
Stating exclusions sets clear boundaries and helps prevent misunderstandings that lead to scope creep.

questions.question: In predictive project management, a baseline is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: A baseline is the approved version of a scope, schedule, or cost plan against which performance is measured, and it can be changed only through formal change control. It is controlled rather than frozen, so calling it unchangeable is inaccurate. Actual results are compared against the baseline but are not the baseline, and a rough draft made before approval has not yet become a baseline.  Takeaway: A baseline is an approved, controlled plan changed only through formal change control, not a frozen document.
choices: An approved scope, schedule, or cost plan that can be changed only through formal change control
The most recent set of actual results and measurements recorded to date
An informal rough draft of the plan produced before stakeholder review
A permanently frozen version of the plan that can never be altered under any circumstances at all

questions.question: When identifying resources for an activity, a team specifies that it needs three testers and one automation tool. This description captures the resources'...
questions.explanation: Stating three testers and one tool defines how many resources are needed (number) and what kind they are (type), which is how resource requirements are described. Cost, schedule, risk, and scope are separate planning dimensions and are not what 'three testers and one tool' expresses.  Takeaway: Resource needs are defined by both the number and the type required.
choices: number and type
cost and schedule
quality and scope
risk and impact

questions.question: Meridian Bank is managing a mobile-app rebuild, a new payments API, and two connected security upgrades together, because coordinating them delivers faster, safer digital banking that none could achieve alone. What is this grouping best called?
questions.explanation: A program is a group of related projects and activities managed in a coordinated way to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually, which fits these interdependent banking initiatives. A portfolio groups components chosen to advance strategy and they need not be related, so it does not capture the tight relationship here; a single project would not contain several distinct initiatives.  Takeaway: Related components managed together for a shared benefit form a program.
choices: A project, because the effort produces one combined digital-banking result for the whole bank.
A portfolio, because several strategic initiatives are being funded and managed at the same time.
An operation, because the coordinated work supports the bank's ongoing day-to-day services.
A program, because related components are managed together to gain benefits not available by managing them separately.

questions.question: A project manager sets a compelling vision and earns the team's trust to inspire extra effort. Which capability is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Inspiring people through vision and earned trust is leadership, which works through influence rather than formal authority. Management relies on systems and positional authority, and it complements leadership rather than being the same capability shown here.  Takeaway: Leadership inspires through vision and earned influence; management relies on systems and position.
choices: Governance, exercised through audit checkpoints
Procurement, exercised through contract control
Management, exercised through positional authority and controls
Leadership, exercised through vision and earned influence

questions.question: A project manager feels a surge of anger during a heated meeting but chooses to pause, breathe, and respond calmly rather than react. Which emotional intelligence capability is this?
questions.explanation: Choosing how to respond to a strong emotion is self-management, which is about regulating the emotion rather than bottling it up. Empathy concerns understanding others, and self-awareness only recognizes the feeling; acting on it constructively is the self-management step.  Takeaway: Self-management means regulating emotions, not bottling them up.
choices: Empathy directed toward the other people in the room
Self-awareness operating entirely on its own
Social skill demonstrated through relationship networking
Self-management, regulating the emotion rather than suppressing it

questions.question: A CIO oversees a collection that holds two programs, four unrelated standalone projects, and some ongoing operational work, and funds or cancels components based on strategic priorities. The components need not relate to one another. What is this collection?
questions.explanation: A portfolio is a collection of projects, programs, subsidiary portfolios, and operations managed together to achieve strategic objectives, and its components need not be related, which matches this strategy-driven mix. A program requires related components working toward a shared benefit, so it does not fit an intentionally unrelated set.  Takeaway: A strategy-driven mix of possibly unrelated components is a portfolio.
choices: A project phase, because funding decisions are made in stages.
A program, because multiple projects are managed together.
A portfolio, because it groups projects, programs, and operations to advance strategy.
A single large project, because one leader oversees it.

questions.question: A project manager is asked whether they can authorize their own project by signing the charter. What is the correct understanding?
questions.explanation: The project manager may help develop the charter and is responsible for integrating and delivering the work, but authorization comes from the sponsor, not from self-signing. The approach used does not change this, and the team does not authorize the charter either.  Takeaway: The PM helps develop and executes the charter; the sponsor authorizes it.
choices: Yes, the project manager fully authorizes the project by signing its charter
Yes, but only when the project follows an adaptive approach
No, only the delivery team is allowed to authorize the charter
No, the PM helps develop and delivers the work but does not authorize the charter

questions.question: A team using MoSCoW is running low on capacity and cannot deliver everything planned for a fixed-date release. Which category should it reduce first to protect the deadline?
questions.explanation: MoSCoW protects a fixed date by sacrificing the least critical work first. Could-haves are desirable but expendable, so they are trimmed before Should-haves, which carry more value. Must-haves are non-negotiable for a viable release, and Won't-have items were already excluded from this release, so neither can be the first thing dropped.  Takeaway: Under deadline pressure, MoSCoW teams drop Could-haves first, then Should-haves, while Must-haves stay in scope.
choices: Must-have items, since dropping them has the smallest impact on the release
Won't-have items, which are the obvious first choice to remove
Could-have items, which are desirable but the least critical to the release
Should-have items, because they are less essential than Could-have items

questions.question: What does the 100 percent rule for a WBS require?
