questions.explanation: The 100 percent rule states that a WBS captures all of the work in scope and no more, so the child elements beneath any parent add up to exactly 100 percent of that parent's work. It is a rule about completeness of scope decomposition, not about member approval, sequencing of packages, or spending the full budget, all of which describe unrelated ideas.  Takeaway: The 100 percent rule: child elements sum to all of the parent's work, capturing the full scope and nothing extra.
choices: The project is required to consume one hundred percent of its approved budget
The work at each child level must sum to one hundred percent of its parent's work, capturing all scope
One hundred percent of the team members must formally approve each work package before any work can start
Each work package must be one hundred percent complete before the next one may begin

questions.question: A project will change how invoices are handled. The team needs to know who is accountable for the invoicing process's overall performance versus who runs it day to day. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: The process owner is accountable for how well a process performs, while the process manager runs it day to day. The reversed pairing swaps those two roles, and the other options assign process accountability to people who do not hold it.  Takeaway: Process owner is accountable for the process; process manager runs it daily.
choices: The process manager is accountable for the process's performance; the process owner runs it day to day.
The product owner is accountable for the process; the project manager runs it day to day.
The process owner is accountable for the process's performance; the process manager runs it day to day.
The sponsor is accountable for the process; the business analyst runs it day to day.

questions.question: Six months after a new self-service portal went live, adoption is far below the business target set in the business case. From a business analysis perspective, what should happen?
questions.explanation: Business analysis extends beyond delivery: solution evaluation measures the deployed product against the value promised in the business case and recommends changes when benefits fall short. Believing the work ends at accepted requirements, renegotiating old sign-offs, or dismissing adoption as purely operational all ignore the analyst's responsibility to confirm that real business value is realized.  Takeaway: Business analysis includes evaluating the live solution against expected business value, not stopping at delivered requirements.
choices: Treat low adoption as an operations problem outside any business analysis responsibility
Reopen the original requirements sign-off and renegotiate the acceptance criteria
Evaluate the deployed solution against the expected business value and recommend adjustments
Consider the analyst's work complete because the requirements were delivered and accepted

questions.question: A recurring defect keeps reaching customers. Before proposing fixes, the project manager insists the team first agree on a clear, specific statement of the problem itself. Why is defining the problem first the right move in structured problem-solving?
questions.explanation: Structured problem-solving starts by defining the problem clearly, because a vague or wrong problem statement sends analysis and solutions in the wrong direction. Only after the real problem and its root cause are understood can the team evaluate options and pick a fix that resolves it, rather than treating a symptom.  Takeaway: Define the problem precisely before generating solutions, so effort targets the real root cause.
choices: Defining the problem is a formality that can be skipped once a plausible fix has been suggested
Problem definition is the sponsor's job, not something the team should spend time on
A precisely defined problem focuses analysis on the real issue and its root cause, so the chosen solution actually addresses it
The first solution proposed is usually correct, so time spent defining the problem is wasted

questions.question: A project team grows from 5 members to 8 members, and every member communicates directly with all the others. Using the communication channels formula, how many additional channels does this growth create?
questions.explanation: The number of communication channels equals n(n-1)/2. With 5 members there are 5x4/2 = 10 channels; with 8 members there are 8x7/2 = 28. The growth adds 28 - 10 = 18 channels. Reporting 28 forgets to subtract the original channels, and 21 comes from using 7 instead of 8 as n.  Takeaway: Communication channels grow as n(n-1)/2, so adding members increases channels far faster than headcount.

questions.question: A large program coordinates many agile teams working toward a shared set of objectives. In a scaling framework such as SAFe, what is the name of the cadence-based planning cycle these teams plan together?
questions.explanation: In SAFe, teams on an Agile Release Train plan together for a Planning Interval, a cadence-based cycle spanning multiple iterations. A single Daily Scrum, a change board, and a closeout phase do not describe this planning cycle.  Takeaway: In SAFe, multiple teams plan together for a Planning Interval (PI).
choices: A project closeout phase
A single Daily Scrum for all of the teams
A combined change control board review
A Planning Interval (PI)

questions.question: A sponsor asks how the team will demonstrate real progress on an adaptive project. What is the best evidence of progress?
questions.explanation: Progress in adaptive work is shown by working, usable increments that meet the Definition of Done. Documents, logged hours, and started-but-unfinished tasks do not demonstrate delivered value.  Takeaway: Real adaptive progress is a working, usable, Done increment.
choices: The total hours logged across the team
The count of tasks marked as started
Working, usable, Done increments of the product
The number of pages in the requirements document

questions.question: A formal requirements agreement must be preserved as an accurate, detailed record that can be referenced later. Which communication choice best meets this need?
questions.explanation: Written communication is best when detail and a durable record matter, because it preserves precise wording that can be referenced later. Conversations, unarchived chats, and phone calls captured only from memory do not leave a reliable, detailed record.  Takeaway: Use written communication when detail and a durable record matter.
choices: A quick instant-message exchange that is not archived.
Written communication that documents the detail for the record.
A phone call summarized only from memory afterward.
A hallway conversation with the key stakeholder.

questions.question: A design team builds a rough version of one dashboard, then reworks that same dashboard over repeated cycles from feedback until it is right. Which approach is this?
questions.explanation: Iterative development refines and improves the same deliverable through successive cycles until it meets the need. Incremental delivery differs because it adds new usable pieces rather than reworking the same one; a fixed up-front design describes predictive work.  Takeaway: Iterative means repeatedly refining the same deliverable.
choices: Incremental, because usable pieces are added each time.
Iterative, because the same work is refined through repeated cycles.
Hybrid, because two approaches are combined.
Predictive, because the design is fixed in advance.

questions.question: A new analyst joins a project that replaces a legacy system and wants to understand existing rules and past pitfalls before meeting stakeholders. Which approach best fits this starting point?
questions.explanation: Document analysis of existing materials together with a lessons-learned review surfaces current rules and known pitfalls, which is the right groundwork before engaging people. Holding a workshop with no preparation is premature, and dismissing documents ignores a valuable source of existing rules.  Takeaway: Start with document analysis and lessons learned to understand existing rules and past pitfalls.
choices: Observing users, on the assumption that documents are never useful.
Document analysis of existing materials plus a review of lessons learned.
Running a large stakeholder workshop before doing any preparation.
Sending a survey to executives asking them to list the system rules.

questions.question: A team using an adaptive (agile) approach asks whether milestones still apply to their work. What is the most accurate response?
questions.explanation: A milestone is a zero-duration significant point, and such points (for example, a release or a major review) exist in adaptive approaches just as in predictive ones. Milestones are not tied to a sprint length, and they do not substitute for the backlog, which holds the work items.  Takeaway: Milestones are significant zero-duration points and appear in adaptive approaches too.
choices: Milestones exist in adaptive approaches too, marking significant points such as a release
Milestones in adaptive work must always last exactly one sprint
Milestones replace the need for a product backlog
Milestones are only a predictive concept and are dropped in adaptive work

questions.question: A stakeholder is upset about a decision. The project manager acknowledges and genuinely understands the stakeholder's feelings while still upholding the agreed decision. This shows that empathy...
questions.explanation: Empathy is understanding another person's perspective and feelings, which does not oblige the manager to agree or to change the decision. It is not the same as pity, and understanding others is a strength rather than something to avoid.  Takeaway: Empathy is understanding another's perspective, not agreeing with it.
choices: means understanding another's perspective without necessarily agreeing
requires the project manager to reverse the decision
is identical to sympathy and offering pity
should be avoided so the manager stays objective

questions.question: Early in discovery, a team wants to generate as many possible feature ideas as it can without judging them yet. Which technique fits this goal?
questions.explanation: Brainstorming is built to generate a large volume of ideas quickly before any are evaluated, which matches the goal of producing many options without early judgment. An interview draws depth from one person, and observation studies existing behavior rather than inventing new possibilities.  Takeaway: Use brainstorming to generate many ideas quickly before evaluating them.
choices: A formal sign-off review of the baselined requirements.
A structured one-on-one interview with a single user.
Observation of users performing their current tasks.
A brainstorming session to generate a wide range of ideas.

questions.question: A business analyst completes the business case and concludes that expected costs outweigh the benefits. Which statement about the business case is correct?
questions.explanation: A business case justifies whether a project is worthwhile and can legitimately recommend not proceeding when costs exceed benefits. It does not authorize the work; that is the charter's role, and the two are separate documents.  Takeaway: A business case can legitimately recommend not proceeding.
choices: It removes the need to create a separate project charter
It automatically authorizes the project work to begin
It can legitimately recommend not proceeding with the project
It must always recommend proceeding once it has been requested

questions.question: Choose TWO items that are typically recorded in the risk register.
questions.explanation: The risk register captures each identified risk with its description and combines probability and impact into a rating used to prioritize responses. The budget baseline belongs to the cost plan, and the acceptance certificate is a closure record, so neither is part of the risk register.  Takeaway: The risk register captures each risk plus its probability and impact rating for prioritization.
choices: The identified risk and its description
The approved project budget baseline
The risk's probability and impact rating
The organization's mission statement
The signed customer acceptance certificate

questions.question: A design team creates one rough wireframe and then repeatedly refines that same wireframe from feedback until it is polished. This way of working is best described as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Iterative work refines the same deliverable repeatedly to improve it. Incremental work instead adds new usable slices, and a single end hand-off describes a predictive delivery.  Takeaway: Iterative means refining the same thing; incremental means adding usable pieces.
choices: A single predictive hand-off at the very end
Parallel delivery of unrelated products
Incremental delivery of separate usable features
Iterative refinement of the same deliverable

questions.question: At the end of a project, the completed product is handed over to the operations group that will run and maintain it. This handover is best described as...
questions.explanation: Moving the finished product to the group that will operate and maintain it is a transition, a normal part of closing. A workaround addresses an unplanned risk, and a change request alters the baseline, so neither describes a planned handover to operations.  Takeaway: Closure includes transitioning the product to operations or the customer.
choices: A change request to the baseline
A transition of the product to the operations group
A workaround for an unplanned problem
A risk response strategy

questions.question: An agile team using fixed iterations discovers new work partway through an iteration. How should the team most appropriately handle the fixed timebox?
questions.explanation: Iteration-based agile uses fixed timeboxes that are not extended or shortened to fit changing work; new items are ordered into a future iteration. Changing the length of the timebox breaks the cadence the team relies on.  Takeaway: In iteration-based agile the timebox length stays fixed; new work goes to a later iteration.
choices: Keep the iteration length fixed and consider the new work for a later iteration
Add the new work to the current iteration without discussion
Immediately shorten the iteration to force completion
Extend the current iteration until the new work is finished

questions.question: Which set of artifacts is most characteristic of documenting project controls on a predictive, plan-based project?
questions.explanation: Predictive control relies on approved baselines for scope, schedule, and cost, supported by registers such as the risk register and by status and performance reports that compare actuals against those baselines. The other sets, backlogs and burndown, Kanban boards and cycle time, and story maps and velocity, are artifacts associated with adaptive delivery rather than predictive, plan-based control.  Takeaway: Predictive control artifacts center on baselines, registers, and performance reports; backlogs and burndowns are adaptive.
choices: User story map, velocity chart, and iteration retrospective notes
Scope, schedule, and cost baselines, a risk register, and performance reports
Kanban board, cycle-time chart, and a team definition of done
Product backlog, sprint backlog, and a sprint burndown chart for the iteration

questions.question: A support team switches to a Kanban approach to manage a continuous flow of incoming tickets. Which TWO practices are core to this flow-based approach? (Choose TWO.)
questions.explanation: Kanban is flow-based and relies on limiting work in progress and pulling new work as capacity frees up. Fixed iterations, Sprint Goals, and Sprint Reviews belong to iteration-based Scrum, not Kanban.  Takeaway: Kanban is flow-based: limit work in progress and pull work as capacity allows.
choices: Committing to fixed-length iterations with a Sprint Goal
Limiting work in progress to improve flow
Assigning story points to forecast a velocity each iteration
Pulling new work only when capacity frees up
Holding a mandatory Sprint Review to approve scope

questions.question: A new agile team reuses its company's shared Definition of Done template and internal coding standards from an earlier project. These shared internal items are best classified as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Organizational process assets are internal items such as templates, standards, and lessons the project can use. Market conditions and regulations sit outside the team's control, and enterprise environmental factors are conditions the team does not control.  Takeaway: Internal templates, standards, and processes the team can use are organizational process assets.
choices: Enterprise environmental factors
Government regulations
Organizational process assets
External market conditions

questions.question: A plan states 'we assume the client will supply test data by week 3' and also 'the budget must not exceed $200,000.' How are these two statements classified?
questions.explanation: An assumption is something taken to be true without proof, matching the belief that data will arrive by week 3, while a constraint is a limiting factor, matching the fixed budget cap. Reversing the two, or forcing both into one category, misapplies the definitions.  Takeaway: Taken as true without proof is an assumption; a limiting factor is a constraint.
choices: The test-data statement is an assumption taken as true without proof, while the budget cap is a constraint that limits it.
Both are assumptions, because each one is simply written down as a statement in the plan.
The test-data statement is really a constraint on the work, while the fixed budget cap is actually just an assumption.
Both are constraints, because each statement could end up limiting how the work is done.

questions.question: A project schedule shows a marker labeled 'Design approved.' It has no work assigned to it and consumes no time. What is this marker best called?
questions.explanation: A milestone is a significant point or event in a project with zero duration; 'Design approved' fits because no work or time is attached to it. A summary activity rolls up child activities and therefore has duration, and a work package is a deliverable that carries associated work.  Takeaway: A milestone marks a significant point in time and has zero duration.
choices: A summary activity
A critical path
A work package
A milestone

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely recorded in the stakeholder register?
questions.explanation: The stakeholder register identifies stakeholders and captures details such as their name, role, and interest in the project. Activity sequencing lives in the schedule, and probability ratings belong to the risk register, not the stakeholder register.  Takeaway: The stakeholder register captures who stakeholders are and their interests.
choices: The earned value of completed work
The probability rating of each identified risk
A stakeholder's name, role, and interest in the project
The sequence of the schedule activities

questions.question: On a predictive project, in which process are completed deliverables formally accepted by the customer or sponsor?
questions.explanation: Validate Scope is the Monitoring and Controlling process where the customer or sponsor formally accepts completed deliverables. Control Quality checks whether deliverables are correct and complete and normally precedes acceptance, but it does not obtain formal sign-off. Close Project or Phase finalizes the project or phase after acceptance has already occurred, so it is not where deliverables are accepted.  Takeaway: Formal acceptance of deliverables happens in Validate Scope, a Monitoring and Controlling process.
choices: Close Project or Phase, performed during Closing
Validate Scope, performed during Monitoring and Controlling
Direct and Manage Project Work, performed during the Executing process group
Control Quality, performed during Executing

questions.question: In which organizational structure does the project manager typically have the LEAST authority, with team members reporting primarily to their functional managers?
questions.explanation: In a functional (hierarchical) organization, staff are grouped by specialty and report to functional managers, so the project manager has little formal authority and often acts more as a coordinator. A projectized structure gives the project manager high authority because the team reports to that manager. Matrix structures share authority to varying degrees, more than functional but less than projectized.  Takeaway: Project manager authority is lowest in functional structures and highest in projectized structures, with matrix in between.
choices: Functional (hierarchical) organization
Balanced matrix organization structure
Strong matrix organization structure
Projectized (fully project-based) organization

questions.question: A team delivers a product in successive slices, and each slice is a complete, usable portion of the final scope that the customer can begin using right away. Which approach does this describe?
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery builds the product in usable pieces, each adding functionality the customer can start using. Iterative delivery instead refines the same work over repeated cycles, and a single final release is characteristic of predictive or waterfall delivery.  Takeaway: Incremental delivery means usable pieces are added over time.
choices: Iterative, because the same feature is refined repeatedly.
Predictive, because everything ships in one final release.
Incremental, because each delivery adds a usable piece of the final product.
Waterfall, because phases run strictly in sequence.

questions.question: Which document describes HOW the project will be executed, monitored, and controlled, integrating the baselines and subsidiary management plans, rather than describing the product itself?
questions.explanation: The project management plan defines how the project is executed, monitored, and controlled by integrating the baselines and the subsidiary management plans. The product management plan concerns the product being built, while the business case and product backlog serve different purposes.  Takeaway: The project management plan is how to manage the project: baselines plus subsidiary plans.
choices: The project business case.
The product backlog.
The project management plan.
The product management plan.

questions.question: When choosing which ready backlog item to work on next, a team wants to prioritize well. Which statement best reflects sound prioritization?
questions.explanation: Prioritization chooses the highest-priority item that is ready, and priority reflects value together with risk, urgency, dependencies, and effort rather than value alone. Picking purely by value, by ease, or by original order ignores the other factors that determine true priority.  Takeaway: Prioritize by overall priority (value plus risk, urgency, dependencies, effort), not by value alone.
choices: Select whichever item is easiest and quickest to complete first, purely to build early momentum
Always select the item with the highest business value, regardless of risk, effort, or dependencies
Select the highest-priority ready item, weighing value along with risk, urgency, dependencies, and effort
Select items strictly in the original order they were written, without reassessing their priority

questions.question: Which sequence correctly reflects the order in which these two documents are typically developed?
questions.explanation: The business case is developed first to justify the project, and the charter follows to authorize it and grant the project manager authority. Reversing the order or treating the business case as unnecessary ignores that justification precedes authorization.  Takeaway: The business case justifies the project before the charter authorizes it.
choices: The two are always developed at exactly the same time
The charter is developed first, then the business case
The business case is developed first, then the charter
Only the charter is developed; the business case is optional

questions.question: What is the purpose and timebox of the Daily Scrum?
questions.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress and plan the next day toward the Sprint Goal. It is not a lengthy stakeholder status meeting or a sign-off gate.
choices: A monthly review where the sponsor signs off on scope
An open-ended session with no time limit for the whole company
A 60-minute status meeting run by the Scrum Master for stakeholders
A 15-minute event for the Developers to plan the next day of work toward the Sprint Goal

questions.question: A sponsor asks about the main trade-off of adopting an adaptive approach rather than a fully predictive plan. Which statement describes an accepted trade-off?
questions.explanation: Adaptive work embraces change and delivers value early, but the exact final scope is less certain at the start. Adaptive work still requires planning and depends heavily on frequent stakeholder feedback.  Takeaway: Adaptive trades up-front scope certainty for the ability to respond to change.
choices: It welcomes change but gives less certainty about final scope up front
It removes the need to gather any stakeholder feedback
It fixes scope early and removes the need to plan at all
It guarantees a lower cost and an earlier fixed deadline

questions.question: Which of the following would be scheduled with a duration greater than zero?
questions.explanation: Configuring the test servers is an activity that consumes work periods, so it carries a duration greater than zero. The other three describe significant points that are reached instantaneously, which are milestones with zero duration.  Takeaway: Activities consume work periods; milestones mark points and have zero duration.
choices: Configure the test servers
Project kickoff completed
Design documents signed off
Phase gate review passed

questions.question: A team wants to express a backlog item using the standard user story structure. Which statement follows that structure correctly?
questions.explanation: The user story template is 'As a <role>, I want <capability>, so that <benefit>,' which the returning-customer statement follows. A 'shall' statement is a functional requirement specification, and a preconditions-and-flow description belongs to a use case rather than a user story.  Takeaway: User story format: 'As a <role>, I want <capability>, so that <benefit>.'
choices: Login: verify the credentials, redirect to the dashboard, and lock the account after five attempts
As a returning customer, I want to save my payment method so that I can check out faster
Use case Authenticate Customer: preconditions include an active account and a valid session
The system shall validate the postal code field against a reference table before submission

questions.question: A Developer is blocked because another department has not provided access to a needed test system. What is the most appropriate action for the Scrum Master?
questions.explanation: As a servant leader, the Scrum Master helps cause impediments to be removed so the Developers can make progress. Reassigning as punishment, waiting passively, or doing the Developers' work does not serve the team.  Takeaway: The Scrum Master serves the team by helping remove impediments.
choices: Help cause the impediment to be removed so the Developers can progress
Tell the Developer to wait quietly until the next Sprint
Assign the blocked work to a different Developer as a punishment
Take over the coding task and finish it personally

questions.question: Team members occasionally need to look up detailed API reference material at their own convenience. Which communication method best serves this need?
questions.explanation: Pull communication such as a wiki or repository lets people retrieve large or reference content whenever they need it. Emailing it daily floods inboxes with information most will not use that day, and a verbal briefing leaves nothing to look up later.  Takeaway: Use pull communication - repository or wiki - for reference content accessed on demand.
choices: Interactive communication scheduled as a recurring standing meeting.
Pull communication, such as a wiki or repository people access on demand.
A one-time verbal briefing that leaves no written record.
Push communication that emails the full reference to everyone daily.

questions.question: A team distinguishes two quality concepts: one lists the specific, testable conditions a single backlog item must meet to be accepted, and the other is the shared standard every item must satisfy to be considered complete. Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria are specific, testable, and item-level, while the Definition of Done is a broader completion standard applied across items. Acceptance criteria work in both predictive and adaptive approaches, and the Definition of Done, though prominent in Scrum, is a general concept rather than Scrum-exclusive.  Takeaway: Acceptance criteria are per-item and testable; the Definition of Done is a broad, shared completion standard.
choices: Item-level conditions are the Definition of Done; the shared completion standard is the acceptance criteria
Both terms mean exactly the same thing and are used interchangeably in practice
Item-level conditions apply only in predictive projects; the shared standard applies only in Scrum
Item-level conditions are the acceptance criteria; the shared completion standard is the Definition of Done

questions.question: A new Scrum Master hears the terms capacity and velocity used as if they mean the same thing. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
questions.explanation: Capacity is the amount of effort a team has available in a period, while velocity is the historical amount of Done work completed per iteration. They are related but not interchangeable, and neither is simply a head count.  Takeaway: Capacity is available effort; velocity is historical completed work. They are not the same.
choices: Capacity is the effort available for a period, while velocity is historical Done work per iteration
Velocity is the hours available, while capacity is work completed historically
Both simply measure the number of people on the team
Capacity and velocity are identical measures of team speed

questions.question: A stakeholder asks the team to explain the difference between the product owner and the product manager. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: A product manager typically owns overall product strategy and direction, while a product owner is a Scrum accountability focused on ordering the backlog; exact titles and duties can vary by organization. They are not the same role, and neither one is the funder - that is the sponsor.  Takeaway: Product manager equals product strategy; product owner equals a Scrum accountability that orders the backlog.
choices: They are two labels for the same accountability on every project.
The product manager owns product strategy; the product owner orders the backlog in Scrum.
The product manager orders the sprint backlog; the owner sets long-term strategy.
The product owner funds the product while the product manager delivers it.

questions.question: A project manager learns that a company owned by their spouse is bidding on the project's contract. Which action best aligns with the Code of Ethics?
questions.explanation: The Code requires disclosing conflicts of interest and refraining from decisions where impartiality could be compromised, so disclosing and recusing oneself is correct. Silently approving or automatically rejecting the bid both let the conflict drive the outcome instead of removing the manager from the decision.  Takeaway: Disclose conflicts of interest and recuse yourself from the decision.
choices: Reject the spouse's bid outright, in order to avoid any possible appearance of personal bias.
Disclose the relationship to the appropriate stakeholders and step out of the selection decision.
Approve the spouse's bid quickly, so that no one thinks the manager is deliberately delaying it.
Say nothing about the relationship for now, since no money has actually changed hands yet.

questions.question: Who is appropriately positioned to grant formal acceptance of the project's final deliverables?
questions.explanation: Formal acceptance of deliverables comes from the customer, sponsor, or another authorized authority who has the standing to sign off. A team member, a supplier, or a senior engineer who built the work is not the authority that accepts it.  Takeaway: Final deliverable acceptance comes from the customer, sponsor, or authorized authority.
choices: The most senior engineer on the team
The customer, sponsor, or other authorized authority
Any team member who helped build the deliverable
The vendor that supplied the raw materials

questions.question: A product team uses the Kano model to think about features. Which description matches a Kano 'delighter' (excitement) feature?
questions.explanation: In the Kano model a delighter is an unanticipated feature that raises satisfaction sharply when present yet causes little dissatisfaction when absent. A must-be feature is the basic expectation noticed mainly by its absence, and a performance feature scales satisfaction with the amount provided.  Takeaway: A Kano delighter is an unexpected feature that thrills when present and is not missed when absent.
choices: A feature whose satisfaction rises in direct proportion to how much of it is provided
A feature that customers explicitly rank as their single highest stated priority
A basic expectation whose absence causes strong dissatisfaction but whose presence is barely noticed
An unexpected feature that greatly increases satisfaction when present but is not missed when absent

questions.question: A scheduler must explain to a sponsor why one particular sequence of activities drives the project's finish date. Which statement about the critical path is correct?
questions.explanation: The critical path is the longest-duration path through the schedule network, so it determines the shortest time in which the project can finish; in a simple unconstrained network its activities have zero total float. The shortest/most-float description is backwards, counting activities ignores their durations, and cost does not define the critical path.  Takeaway: Critical path = longest path = shortest possible project duration, typically with zero total float.
choices: It is the shortest path through the network and carries the most total float, so delays on it are easily absorbed.
It is the longest-duration path through the network, and because it is the longest it sets the shortest possible project finish.
It is whichever path contains the greatest number of activities, regardless of how long those activities take.
It is the path with the highest combined cost, so it governs the budget rather than the schedule.

questions.question: Which set correctly lists the three components of the scope baseline?
questions.explanation: The scope baseline is the approved scope statement, the WBS, and the WBS dictionary. Sets that include the charter, schedule, cost baseline, or risk register mix in documents that belong to other baselines or plans.  Takeaway: The scope baseline is the scope statement plus the WBS plus the WBS dictionary.
choices: The scope statement, the schedule baseline, and the cost baseline.
The scope statement, the WBS, and the WBS dictionary.
The project charter, the schedule, and the budget.
The requirements list, the risk register, and the WBS.

questions.question: During planning, a business analyst and the product owner disagree about which requirement should be built first. Who is accountable for deciding the relative business value and priority of the requirements?
questions.explanation: In Scrum the product owner is accountable for ordering the backlog by value, so that priority call is theirs. The analyst elicits and analyzes requirements but does not own value or priority, and the sponsor funds the work rather than ranking each individual item.  Takeaway: The analyst supports requirements; the product owner owns value and backlog priority in agile.
choices: The project manager, because they control the schedule and the budget.
The business analyst, because they elicited and documented the requirements.
The product owner, because ordering the backlog by value is their accountability.
The sponsor, because they must personally rank every backlog item.

questions.question: During planning, a team notes that a new data-privacy law and the current hiring market for developers both shape how it will work. These two items are best classified as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Enterprise environmental factors are conditions outside the team's control, such as laws and labor-market conditions. Assets the team owns and can change are organizational process assets, and backlog stories are work items, not conditions.  Takeaway: Conditions outside the team's control, like laws and market forces, are enterprise environmental factors.
choices: Organizational process assets the team owns
Enterprise environmental factors outside the team's control
User stories placed in the product backlog
Items the team can freely change through governance

questions.question: A team uses MoSCoW to prioritize scope for a timeboxed release. Which statement about MoSCoW is accurate?
questions.explanation: In MoSCoW the 'W' means Won't-have-this-time, which defers an item from the current release while leaving it available for a future one. There is no fixed percentage cap on Must-haves, and Should-haves are important but not mandatory for acceptance.  Takeaway: MoSCoW 'W' means Won't-have-this-time (deferred, not rejected); there is no fixed Must-have cap.
choices: Should-have items are mandatory, and the release cannot be accepted without them
'Won't-have-this-time' defers an item from the current release without rejecting it forever
Must-have items are capped at a fixed percentage of the total scope by rule
The 'W' stands for 'Would-be-nice,' which permanently rejects the item from the product

questions.question: A business analyst is deciding when to run a facilitated workshop. Select the TWO situations where a workshop is the most appropriate elicitation technique.
questions.explanation: Workshops are designed to build agreement and resolve conflict among a group of stakeholders gathered together, which fits both resolving a cross-department dispute and reaching shared agreement on scope. Probing one expert in depth is an interview, and gathering input from thousands of users points to a survey. A one-on-one interview probes a single expert in depth, a survey collects quick input from very large groups, and reviewing existing manuals is document analysis - none of those is a facilitated group workshop.  Takeaway: Use workshops to build agreement and resolve conflict among stakeholders.
choices: Resolving conflicting requirements between two departments.
Probing one expert's detailed reasoning in depth.
Building shared agreement on scope among key stakeholders.
Collecting quick input from several thousand end users.
Documenting an already well-understood process by reviewing existing reference manuals.

questions.question: Which document formally authorizes the existence of a project and empowers the project manager to apply organizational resources to project activities?
questions.explanation: The project charter formally authorizes the project and gives the project manager the authority to apply organizational resources. The project management plan describes how the project will be executed and is developed after the charter authorizes the work. The WBS decomposes the scope, and the business case justifies why the project is worth doing, but neither grants authority.  Takeaway: The project charter authorizes the project and empowers the project manager; the business case only justifies it.
choices: The project charter
The business case
The work breakdown structure
The project management plan

questions.question: Which delivery pattern is most characteristic of a predictive, plan-based project?
questions.explanation: Predictive delivery is planned up front and tends to hand over value in fewer, larger releases tied to milestones or the end of a phase. Continuous deployment, an increment every iteration, and per-requirement releases all describe adaptive delivery cadences, where value is delivered in many small, frequent increments rather than a few planned ones.  Takeaway: Predictive delivery = fewer, larger, planned releases; adaptive delivery = frequent small increments.
choices: Continuous deployment of tiny increments many times per day
A potentially shippable increment released at the end of every short iteration
Fewer, larger releases delivered at planned milestones or phase completions
A release triggered automatically whenever a single requirement is accepted

questions.question: A software upgrade project has clear, stable requirements, a well-understood technical solution, and very little change expected during delivery. Which development approach best fits these conditions?
questions.explanation: A predictive approach fits work whose scope is defined up front and stable, where the solution is known and change is unlikely, so the project can be planned in detail and executed against baselines. Adaptive approaches earn their value when requirements are uncertain or volatile, which is the opposite of the stability described, so that reasoning is wrong. Wanting frequent small increments is a signal for an adaptive cadence, not a justification for predictive.  Takeaway: Predictive fits stable, well-defined scope with low expected change; uncertainty and frequent increments point to adaptive.
choices: Adaptive, because low expected change means the team should re-plan continuously
Predictive, because the sponsor wants a working increment delivered every two weeks
Adaptive, because stable requirements are always best handled through many frequent short iterations
Predictive, plan-based, because the requirements are stable and the solution is well understood

questions.question: A stakeholder asks which of the following is NOT part of the business analyst's responsibilities. Which one should the analyst point to?
questions.explanation: Business analysis covers eliciting, analyzing, documenting, managing, and helping validate requirements, so those are within the analyst's scope. Deciding the budget belongs to the sponsor and setting business priorities belongs to the business, so that is not the analyst's responsibility.  Takeaway: The analyst elicits, analyzes, documents, manages, and helps validate - but does not own budget or business-priority decisions.
choices: Eliciting and analyzing requirements from stakeholders.
Helping validate that requirements meet the real need.
Deciding the project's budget and the final business priorities.
Documenting and managing requirements as they evolve.

questions.question: During execution, a supplier reports that parts already delivered are defective and the assembly line is stopped right now. Is this an issue or a risk?
questions.explanation: An issue is a condition or event that has already happened and requires action now, which fits the defective parts stopping the line. A risk is a future, uncertain event, so it does not describe something that has already occurred.  Takeaway: Already happened is an issue; future and uncertain is a risk.
choices: A constraint, because the defective parts now limit what the project can do.
An assumption, because the team had assumed the delivered parts would be good.
A risk, because the stoppage may end up affecting the project's overall schedule.
An issue, because it is a condition that has already occurred and needs resolution now.

questions.question: A project manager needs to make 400 employees aware of a system cutover date. No discussion is required - only broad awareness. Which method fits best?
questions.explanation: Push communication such as an announcement email or dashboard efficiently broadcasts one-way awareness to a large audience. Interactive calls to 400 people are impractical for a simple notice, and pull methods risk people never looking up the date.  Takeaway: Use push communication - email, report, dashboard - to broadcast awareness to many.
choices: Push communication, such as an announcement email or a dashboard notice.
Pull communication that waits for each employee to search for the date.
A negotiation workshop that gathers all 400 employees at once.
Interactive communication through individual phone calls to each employee.

questions.question: On a team's burnup chart, the completed-work line rises steadily while the total-scope line stays flat, then the scope line suddenly steps up. What most likely caused the scope line to move?
questions.explanation: On a burnup chart the scope line moves only when scope is added, removed, or re-estimated, not when work is completed or items are reordered. Reordering priorities and finishing items affect the completed line or nothing on the scope line at all.  Takeaway: The burnup scope line moves only on scope change or re-estimation, never on reordering.
choices: The team completed several items in one day
A daily standup ran longer than planned
The team reordered existing backlog items by priority
New scope was added to the backlog for the release

questions.question: A team needs to document a full interaction, including who initiates it, what must be true before it starts, the normal sequence of steps, and what happens when something goes wrong. Which artifact fits this need?
questions.explanation: A use case captures a complete interaction, naming actors, preconditions, and the main, alternate, and exception flows. A user story is a small placeholder for a later conversation rather than a full flow, and a traceability matrix records trace links rather than interaction steps.  Takeaway: A full interaction with actors, preconditions, and flows is a use case; a small slice is a user story.
choices: A single user story written on an index card
A theme placed on the product roadmap
A row in the requirements traceability matrix
A use case with actors, preconditions, and main, alternate, and exception flows

questions.question: A risk that the team had planned a response for has just occurred, and the risk register documents the agreed response. What should the project manager do first?
questions.explanation: When a planned response already exists, the project manager follows it rather than improvising. A workaround is reserved for unplanned risks, and neither ignoring the plan nor waiting passively is appropriate when an agreed response is on hand.  Takeaway: For a risk with a planned response, execute the plan; workarounds are for unplanned risks.
choices: Invent a brand-new workaround on the spot
Ignore the plan and escalate to the sponsor at once
Wait to see whether the risk resolves on its own
Implement the response already planned and agreed

questions.question: At a Sprint Review, stakeholders view the increment and give positive feedback. A team member concludes the increment is therefore formally accepted for release. Why is this conclusion questionable?
questions.explanation: Delivery readiness means the required release-scope items are Done against their acceptance criteria and completion standards, with formal acceptance where governance requires it; a demo or Sprint Review is not itself an automatic sign-off gate. It is not true that reviews can only reject work, nor that roadmap dates determine readiness.  Takeaway: A demo or Sprint Review is feedback, not automatic acceptance; readiness is required items Done plus any required formal sign-off.
choices: Because a demo or review is not an automatic sign-off; readiness means required items are Done and any required formal acceptance is obtained
Because a Sprint Review is designed only to reject work and can never approve an increment for release
Because release readiness depends solely on whether the roadmap's planned dates were actually met
Because only the delivery team, and never the reviewing stakeholders, may ever accept an increment
